proposals.claim_text: Light in fibre attenuates with distance through absorption and scattering, so long routes need amplification.
proposals.source_title: The FOA Reference For Fiber Optics - Optical Fiber
proposals.snippet: The attenuation of the optical fiber is a result of two factors, absorption and scattering.
proposals.proposed_text: Light in a fibre is weakened by absorption and scattering in the glass, so long links use in-line amplifiers to compensate for the losses.
proposals.notes: The same section later states 'The largest cause of attenuation is scattering.' and that scattering is 'proportional to the inverse fourth power of the wavelength', which is Rayleigh behaviour, though the page does not use the word 'Rayleigh'. Amplification need: RP Photonics EDFA page says 'Using multiple amplifiers in a long fiber-optic link has the advantage that large transmission losses can be compensated' (https://www.rp-photonics.com/erbium_doped_fiber_amplifiers.html). Corning was not checked.

extra_evidence.title: Propagation losses
extra_evidence.location: Section on intrinsic vs. extrinsic losses
extra_evidence.snippet: For example, silica fibers exhibit some intrinsic losses due to infrared absorption and also due to Rayleigh scattering at unavoidable inhomogeneities of the glass.

proposals.claim_text: Erbium-doped fibre amplifiers, pumped by a laser, amplify the optical signal directly without electrical conversion.
proposals.source_title: David N. Payne
proposals.source_publisher: IEEE History Center / Engineering and Technology History Wiki (ETHW)
proposals.snippet: Still by far the most successful optical amplifier, the EDFA, pumped by a tiny diode laser, allows the optical signals carrying Internet data to be periodically boosted within the fiber itself. This eliminated the need for expensive, capacity-choking, electronic signal regenerators
proposals.proposed_text: An erbium-doped fibre amplifier, pumped by a small diode laser, boosts the light signal within the fibre itself, removing the need for electronic regenerators.
proposals.notes: The snippet ends mid-sentence, a truncation of verbatim text. 'Without converting to electrical' is implied by 'eliminated the need for ... electronic signal regenerators'; entry 2 states the electrical conversion explicitly.

extra_evidence.title: Underwater Cables

proposals.claim_text: Operators reroute traffic over other cables and paths when one cable fails.
proposals.source_title: Submarine Cable FAQs (TeleGeography)
proposals.snippet: You rarely hear about these cable faults because most companies that use cables follow a “safety in numbers” approach to usage, spreading their networks' capacity across multiple cables so that if one breaks, their network will continue to run smoothly over the other cables while service is restored on the damaged one.
proposals.proposed_text: Most companies spread their capacity across several cables, so when one breaks, traffic keeps flowing over the others while the damaged cable is repaired.
proposals.notes: TeleGeography describes spreading capacity across several cables, which is not quite the same as operators actively rerouting traffic after a failure. The proposed text follows the source. Mechanism corroboration from the Wikipedia Submarine communications cable article (verbatim): 'A further redundant-path development over and above the self-healing rings approach is the mesh network whereby fast switching equipment is used to transfer services between network paths with little to no effect on higher-level protocols if a path becomes inoperable.' Not every user is protected: the same FAQ says countries need multiple cables for reliable connectivity, so places with only one cable can still lose service.
